title: Do cold feet give you a cold? Scientists tested it
description:
Colds are caused by viruses, and earlier studies found no link to getting chilled. Then in 2005 Cardiff University's Common Cold Centre put 90 volunteers' feet in icy water for 20 minutes: 13 of them reported a cold in the next 4-5 days, against 5 of the 90 whose feet sat in an empty bowl. The researchers' theory: the virus was already there, and the chill weakened the nose's defences.

Sources:
- Acute cooling of the feet and the onset of common cold symptoms (Johnson & Eccles, Family Practice 2005): PubMed record — National Library of Medicine (PubMed): https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=16286463&rettype=abstract&retmode=text
- Study: Chills can trigger colds — CNN: https://edition.cnn.com/2005/HEALTH/11/14/cold.chill/index.html
- Feeling a Chill Can Brrrr-ing on a Cold — HealthDay: https://www.healthday.com/health-news/pulmonology/feeling-a-chill-can-brrrr-ing-on-a-cold-529127.html
- Common cold — NHS: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/common-cold/

This is one study of 180 people; the mechanism is the researchers' theory, and the authors said further studies are needed. Press reports at the time quoted 29% vs 9%; the numbers here are from the paper's abstract. The characters are cartoons, not medical advice. Narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro-82M).
